Asteroid Belt. The Asteroid Belt is a region of space between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter populated by millions of rocky objects ranging from dust particles to dwarf planets. Often imagined as a dense field of colliding rocks, the belt is actually sparse—spacecraft navigate it routinely without collision risk. It is thought to be a remnant of the solar system's formation, representing material that never coalesced into a planet, likely due to Jupiter's gravitational influence.

The asteroid belt contains approximately one point nine million objects larger than one kilometer in diameter, with a combined mass less than Earth's Moon. The dwarf planet Ceres, located in the asteroid belt's inner region, is the largest object and comprises roughly one-third of the belt's total mass.

The belt extends roughly from two point two to three point two astronomical units from the Sun, with objects orbiting in periods between three and six years. Jupiter's gravity is thought to have prevented asteroids from accreting into a planet. Gravitational perturbations can eject objects into the inner solar system, creating meteorites, or propel them outward.

Notable asteroids include Vesta, which is large, bright, and geologically complex. Eros is an elongated, potato-shaped object visited by NASA's NEAR-Shoemaker spacecraft. Apophis is a near-Earth asteroid whose trajectory has been carefully monitored. Spectroscopic studies classify asteroids into types—carbonaceous, or C-type, which are dark and carbon-rich; silicate-rich, or S-type; and metallic-rich, or M-type—reflecting different solar-system formation environments.

NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited both Vesta and Ceres, revealing them as differentiated bodies with complex geological histories.
